newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GOVT APPROVES FURTHER FLOOD RELIEF FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GOVT APPROVES FURTHER FLOOD RELIEF FUNDS.

text.p: The Czech government on Wednesday approved the distribution of a further 1.9 billion crowns ($56.1 million) from the state budget to help pay for communication and ecological problems caused by recent flooding.
Speaking after a regular government meeting, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said the government would also request some 2.3 billion crowns in aid from the European Union through its PHARE programme.

Klaus said that some 660 million crowns would be earmarked for the repair of local communications, while another 600 million crowns would be given to help rebuild the communications sector in general.
He added that 150 million crowns would be extended to help solve ecological problems resulting from the flooding.
Five hundred million crowns from the state budget -- in addition to 150 million from other sources -- would go to rebuilding housing.

"We have some unused money from PHARE that we have accumulated over the past year to a maximum of 2.3 billion crowns and the government has requested Finance Minister Ivan Pilip to quickly deal with Brussels about transforming it from its original usage," Klaus said.
He did not say what purpose the funds originally had.
Severe flooding caused by torrential rains last month devastated parts of the east of the Czech Republic, as well as parts of western Poland, killing some 100 people.
Officials say Czech river levels have since receded, with most areas now out of danger.
A Czech government crisis team on Monday estimated total damage from the floods at 60 billion crowns.

Apart from approving the issue of some five billion crowns worth of flood bonds, the government has pledged around five billion crowns in privatisation proceeds and is considering a loan of more than 10 billion crowns from the European Investment Bank.
The floods destroyed thousands of homes, businesses and crops, costing billions of dollars throughout the region.
The official Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) has said the flooding would mean that Czech real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for the year would be at the low end of its 2.0 to 3.0 percent range.
But Ivan Sujan, vice-chairman of the CSU, has said that his personal estimate was for GDP growth of only 1.5 to 2.0 percent.
